title: The Baboon Troop That Turned Peaceful
text:
For years the neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky studied wild olive baboons in Kenya, including a group he called Forest Troop. Like most baboon troops, it was ruled by aggressive adult males who regularly attacked lower-ranking males and females.

In the early 1980s the troop began raiding a rubbish dump at a tourist lodge. Only the most aggressive males fought their way into the dump, and the meat there was contaminated with tuberculosis. Those males died. What was left was a troop with unusually few males, and those who remained were the less aggressive ones.

A decade later, Sapolsky and Lisa Share compared Forest Troop with other troops. Its culture had changed. Males fought less, directed aggression mainly at males of similar rank rather than at the weak, and spent more time near and grooming females. Low-ranking animals showed less sign of physiological stress. Most striking of all, none of the original males were left. The troop's males had arrived as adolescents from other troops, and they had adopted the calmer style, which persisted as each new generation came in.
lesson: A group's culture outlives the people who created it. Who sits at the top sets norms that newcomers absorb, so choose and model the culture you want to last.
source: Sapolsky, R. M., and Share, L. J. (2004). A pacific culture among wild baboons: Its emergence and transmission. PLoS Biology, 2(4), e106.
caveat: It is a single natural event in one troop, so the explanation is strong but cannot be tested by repeating it.
